fufu was written for one working tree. A pool of worktrees is how several agents work at once, and every per-repository assumption — one operation log, one undo pointer, one lock, one ref table — was wrong the moment a repository had two checkouts. This release is that seam, and the surfaces a fleet needs from outside it.

**One chain per worktree**

The operation log moves to `refs/fufu/wt/<id>/ops`, keyed by the worktree's gitdir basename. Each worktree gets its own undo pointer, its own lock, and a ref table holding only the refs it owns — so an undo in one tree no longer reverts another tree's branch, and a read in a bay no longer appends to a chain it does not belong to. Migration is automatic and carries the reflog, so redo survives it.

The chain stays in the shared ref namespace rather than moving under `refs/worktree/`: `git gc` from the main worktree collects objects pinned only by a linked worktree's refs there, and reachability is the whole of fufu's gc pin. That is also what lets a chain outlive its checkout.

**A branch is only ever open in one worktree**

git refuses to check out a branch two worktrees already hold. gix's ref transactions enforce nothing, so fufu carries the check itself — `ff switch`, `ff start` and `ff edit` refuse in git's own words, naming the branch and the path.

`ff restack` moves the branch you named and no other. Everything else the rewrite touched is left where it stood and named in the output. This diverges from `git rebase --update-refs`, which carries every ref in the range: git's rebase assumes exclusive control of the one worktree doing it, and fufu cannot.

**`ff worktree`**

`add`, `list`, `remove`. fufu lays git's on-disk layout itself, so the two tools stay interchangeable.

A creation lays the new worktree's chain floor as it goes, so `ff undo` works in the bay from its first command rather than its second. A removal captures the tree first, into that tree's own chain, which is why there is no `--force`: git demands one for a dirty worktree because it has nowhere to put the work, and fufu put it somewhere a line earlier.

The chain survives the checkout, so the listing closes with the chains whose worktree is gone — each row an address rather than a memorial, since `ff restore <path> --at-op <op>` takes the id directly. That is the agent-deleted-my-bay case, answered by verbs that already existed. `ff undo` reverses either direction, reviving a worktree under its original id with its uncommitted work.

Under `fufu.translate`, `git worktree add` finds the fufu verb. `remove` deliberately does not: fufu's captures the tree first, and a translation that quietly did more than the command asked would be the wrong kind of helpful.

**`ff collide`**

fufu measured a branch on two axes and both pointed vertically — the base beneath it, and the remote copy of itself. Neither answers the question two people working at once actually have.

`ff collide` prints one line per pair of branches, the paths where two of them touch the same thing, and the largest set that touches nothing. Each side is measured by its open change, read from the operation log rather than from a worktree, so a branch checked out somewhere else — or nowhere — still answers, and a name wears a `*` when it has work that has not been committed. Two people editing the same lines see each other before either has committed, which is the half of the day every tracker built on commits is blind to.

**`ff watch`**

Newline-delimited JSON, one object per motion, for status lines, editor plugins and agent supervisors. Not a daemon: a foreground process you started, holding no authority and writing nothing.

A subscriber is not told what was *appended*, because the log does not only append — an undo steps the pointer backwards, a restore across a fork lands on a sibling, a trim rewrites every surviving id. `Start`, `Landed`, `SteppedBack`, `Forked` and `Rewritten` are the closed set of honest answers.

`--all` is one process over every chain in the repository, and a `worktree` field rides every line in both modes. It is an added field, so the contract stays at 1.

**An extension is a binary**

`ff tower next` runs `ff-tower` from PATH, the way git has always found `git-lfs`. No plugin API, no registry, nothing to install into fufu — a name and a directory on PATH is the whole contract. A builtin always wins, and a word that resolves nowhere gets clap's own error back.

The child inherits `FF_REPO`, `FF_CONTRACT` and `FF_SESSION`. The session is what lets one `ff undo` step over a whole flight's captures rather than one keystroke of them.

`ff -C <dir>` (`--cwd`) is git's spelling of the missing flag: a chdir before anything discovers, so a relative path argument after it resolves against `<dir>` too. Any directory inside the repository will do, a linked worktree included, which is how you ask one bay a question without leaving another.

**Smaller things**

`LESS` now defaults to `FR` rather than `FRX`, so the pager enters the alternate screen and the mouse wheel scrolls again. git carries `-X` for a reason that expired with less 530 in 2018.

Worktree paths have one spelling across messages, listings and JSON. Extended-length prefixes on Windows and symlinked temporary directories on macOS no longer produce paths git cannot parse or a person cannot type.

The `tower` sketch now lives at [tyler-johnson/tower](https://github.com/tyler-johnson/tower).

**Numbers**

32 commits over v0.7.0, +8,026/−661 across 78 files. 1,364 workspace tests, up from 1,252. 108 `ff explain` ids, up from 101.
